subject: chemistry

moments.title: Ingold and Hughes formalise
moments.body: At UCL, Ingold and Hughes formalise the SN1/SN2 (and E1/E2) classification of organic reaction mechanisms. They derive rate laws and stereochemical signatures for each. Curly arrows enter undergraduate teaching.

moments.title: Walden inversion explained
moments.body: Hughes and Ingold show SN2 produces inversion of configuration at the stereo centre — explaining the Walden inversion known since 1896. They distinguish 'frontside' vs 'backside' attack.

moments.title: Hughes-Ingold rules
moments.body: Their book systematises solvent and substrate effects on SN1/SN2. The Hughes-Ingold rules predict which mechanism dominates.
moments.takeaway: Mechanism is now predictable from substrate and conditions.

moments.title: Mechanism by computation
moments.body: DFT calculations now compute transition-state energies for arbitrary reactions, predicting selectivity and yield before lab work begins.
moments.takeaway: Curly arrows have become quantum chemistry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: SN1, SN2, E1, E2 are universal teaching frameworks. Modern computation extends to enzymes, materials, polymers.
now.open_questions: Can we computationally predict reaction yields and selectivities for arbitrary substrates?

reflection: Curly arrows are a 1930s graphical convention. They remain the universal language of organic chemistry. Why have they not been replaced by something more rigorous?
